column2: They speak to me with trust and ever restrain me, those who see me devoted to the words of the offerings to the ancestors, obedient and free of envy.
As bees gather honey, the teachers gather one who is righteous-souled, master of anger, restrained and of controlled senses.
So I, tasting the savours ground at the tip of the tongue, stand over my own kind as the moon over the stars.
This is the nectar of the earth, this the unsurpassed eye: the offering to the ancestors in the mouth of a Brahmana; hearing this, one proceeds."
[Dhritarashtra said:] "'This much is the good,' said Prahlada to the expounder of Brahman; served by him, the lord of the Daityas then spoke:
'I am pleased with your service to your teacher as is fitting, best of the twice-born; choose a boon, good luck to you; I shall surely give it.'
'It is done,' the Brahmana said to the lord of the Daityas; but Prahlada said, 'Pleased, let a boon be taken.'
[The Brahmana said:] 'If you are pleased, king, and wish my good, I wish to obtain your good conduct; this is my boon.'
[Dhritarashtra said:] Then the lord of the Daityas was pleased, yet great fear arose in him, since the boon asked by the Brahmana was no small thing.
'So be it,' said Prahlada to him, astonished then; having granted the boon to the Brahmana, he became distressed.
When the boon was given and the Brahmana had gone, great anxiety came upon Prahlada, great king, and he could not reach a resolution.
As he brooded, dear one, a radiance like a shadow, with a body, then left his body.
Prahlada asked that huge form, 'Who are you?' It answered, 'I am Good Conduct; I am abandoned by you and go.
I shall dwell, king, in that best of Brahmanas, blameless, who came to you as a disciple and was ever attentive.' Saying this it vanished, and entered Shakra, lord.
When that radiance had gone, another of the same form came out of his body; he said, 'Who are you?'
'Know me, Prahlada, as Dharma; where that best of Brahmanas is, I shall go, lord of the Daityas; where Good Conduct is, there am I.'
Then another, great king, as if blazing with radiance, came out of the body of the great-souled Prahlada.
Asked, 'Who are you?', that radiant one said to him: 'I am Truth, chief of the Asuras; I shall follow Dharma here.'
When he had gone after Dharma, another person came out of him, and being asked by the great soul, said: 'Know me as Conduct, Prahlada; where truth is, there am I.'
When he had gone, a great white one came out of his body; asked, he said: 'Know me as Strength; where conduct is, there am I.' Having said this, he went where conduct was, lord of men.
Then a radiant goddess came out of his body; the lord of the Daityas asked her, and she said, 'I am Shri.'
'I have lived happily in you, hero, of true valour; abandoned by you I shall go where strength is.'
Then fear arose in the great-souled Prahlada, and he asked her again, 'Where are you going, dweller in the lotus?
You are the goddess true to her vows, supreme sovereign of the world; and who is that best of Brahmanas? I wish to know the truth.'
[Shri said:] 'That is Shakra, the celibate student, whom you taught; the lordship you had over the three worlds was taken by him, lord.
By good conduct you conquered all the worlds, knower of dharma; knowing that, Mahendra took your good conduct, lord.
Dharma, truth, conduct, strength and I are rooted in good conduct, greatly wise one, always; there is no doubt in this.'
[Bhishma said:] Having thus spoken, Shri went, and all those others, Yudhishthira. But Duryodhana said again to his father:
I wish to know the truth of good conduct, delight of the Kurus; and tell me the means by which good conduct is attained.
[Dhritarashtra said:] "The means was stated before by the great-souled Prahlada; hear in brief the attainment of good conduct, lord of men.
Non-hostility toward all beings in deed, mind and speech, and kindness and giving—this is praised as good conduct.
That deed, or manly act, of one's own which would not be good for others, or by which one would be ashamed, one should never do.
Do that deed by which one may be praised in an assembly; this is good conduct told in brief, best of the Kurus.
Even if the ill-conducted somewhere gain fortune, king, they do not enjoy it long, dear one, and fall with their roots.
Knowing this in truth, become of good conduct, my son, if you wish for fortune much greater than Yudhishthira's, dear one."
[Bhishma said:] "This Dhritarashtra told his son, lord of men; do this, son of Kunti, and you will obtain its fruit."

This great doubt has arisen in me, Grandsire, and no one but you can cut it, scourge of foes.
mahabharata:12:125.3	My hope in Suyodhana was great, Grandsire: that when war came he would do what was fitting, lord.
mahabharata:12:125.4	A very great hope arises in every man; when it is struck down, death is painful, without doubt.
mahabharata:12:125.5	I am hopeless, ill-minded, made so by that evil-souled son of Dhritarashtra, king of kings; see my dull-mindedness.
mahabharata:12:125.6	I think hope greater than a mountain with its trees, or even than the sky, king, or again immeasurable.
mahabharata:12:125.7	And this, best of the Kurus, is hard to conceive and very hard to obtain; and seeing that it is hard to obtain, what else is harder than it?
[Bhishma said:] "On this I shall relate to you, Yudhishthira, hear it: the history of Sumitra and of Rishabha.
A royal sage named Sumitra, a Haihaya, went hunting; he pursued a deer, having pierced it with a smooth-jointed arrow.
Then the king, from youth and innate strength, pursued it, bow in hand and sword at side, like a swan.
Crossing streams and rivers, pools and forests, passing beyond one after another, he pursued, ranging the forest.
But the deer, king, at will, coming near the king again and again, fled again at great speed.
Struck by his many arrows, the forest-ranger, as if sporting, king of kings, came near again.
Again taking speed, the swift leader of the herd, passing beyond, king of kings, came near again.
Sumitra, scourge of foes, taking a best arrow, terrible and cutting the vitals, let it loose from the bow.
Then the leader of the herd, at a distance of a gavyuti, leaving the arrow's path, stood as if laughing.
When that arrow fell burning on the ground, the deer entered the great forest and the king too rushed after.
Having entered the great forest, he came to a hermitage of ascetics, and the king, weary, sat down there.
Seeing him with bow, afflicted by weariness and hungry, the sages gathered round and honoured him according to rule.
The sages asked the tiger among kings his purpose: "By what object, good sir, have you come to the penance grove?
On foot, with sword bound on, bow and arrows, lord of men—we wish to know whence you have come, giver of honour. In what family were you born? What is your name? Tell us."
Then the king, bull among men, told all the twice-born, as was fitting, about his attendance, Bharata.

Born in the family of the Haihayas, I am Sumitra, delight of friends. I range killing herds of deer by thousands with arrows, protected by a great army, with ministers and my household.
mahabharata:12:125.26	A deer pierced by my arrow runs with the shaft in it; pursuing it as it fled, I have come by chance to this forest, to your presence, my fortune lost, hopeless, worn out by exertion.
mahabharata:12:125.27	What greater sorrow could there be than this, that I, worn out by exertion, have come to your hermitage, hopeless and my marks lost?
mahabharata:12:125.28	Neither loss of the marks of kingship nor of the city, wealthy ascetics, gives me such sharp pain as the destruction of my hope.
mahabharata:12:125.29	Neither the Himalaya, great mountain, nor the ocean, great sea, in greatness could be compared with it, like the space between heaven and earth; of hope, best of ascetics, I have not reached the end.
mahabharata:12:125.30	All is known to you, for ascetics know all; you are greatly fortunate, therefore I shall ask my doubt.
mahabharata:12:125.31	The hopeful man, or even the sky—what in the world seems greater by its greatness to you? This I wish to hear truly: what here is hard to obtain?
mahabharata:12:125.32	If it is a secret, you who are ever in austerity, do not tell it to me soon; I do not wish to hear a secret, bulls among the twice-born,
mahabharata:12:125.33	or if there be any obstruction to your austerity by which I should cease; or if there is an occasion for this question I have raised.
mahabharata:12:125.34	I wish to hear the whole reason for this truly; for you who are ever in austerity, attentive, may say it.

Long ago, tiger among kings, lord, I was visiting holy places and reached the divine hermitage of Nara and Narayana.
mahabharata:12:126.3	There is that lovely badari tree and the lake Vaihayasa, where Ashvashiras, king, recites the eternal Vedas.
mahabharata:12:126.4	Having duly made offerings in that lake to the ancestors and the gods, I then went to the hermitage.
mahabharata:12:126.5	Where those two sages Nara and Narayana ever delight, I then went to a hermitage not far off to dwell.
mahabharata:12:126.6	Then I saw a sage coming, in bark and deerskin, thin and exceedingly tall, named Tanu, a treasury of austerity.
mahabharata:12:126.7	Compared with other men, mighty-armed, he was eight times thinner in body; such thinness, royal sage, was never seen anywhere.
mahabharata:12:126.8	His body, king of kings, was like a little finger; his neck, arms, feet and hair were wonderful to see.
mahabharata:12:126.9	His head was proportionate to the body, his ears and eyes the same; his speech and movements, best of kings, were ordinary.
mahabharata:12:126.13	While he was speaking, a lotus-eyed king came up with fast horses, with his army and household.
mahabharata:12:126.14	Remembering his son lost in the forest, greatly dejected, the wise father of Bhuridyumna, best of the Raghus, of great fame...
mahabharata:12:126.15	I shall see that son here, I shall see him here," thought the king; thus, made hopeful, king, he ranged this forest long ago.
He is hard for me to see, surely, being highly righteous; my only son was lost in the great forest, he said again and again then.
He is hard for me to see and my hope is great; with it my body is wasted, I wish to die; there is no doubt.
Hearing this, the blessed Tanu, best of eminent sages, stood a moment with head bowed, absorbed in thought.
Seeing him thinking, the king, greatly dejected, spoke in a low voice, miserable, as if again and again:
What is hard to obtain, Brahmana sage, and what is there beyond hope? Let the blessed one say this, if it is no secret from me.
The blessed great sage had once been slighted by him, relying on a foolish judgment, through his own ill fortune.
Asking for a pot, king, gold and bark garments, that Brahmana sage, disgusted, had become hopeless.
So saying, and saluting that sage honoured by the world, the righteous-souled king sat down, weary, like you, best of men.
Then the great sage brought water of welcome and for the feet and offered all to the king by the forest rule.
Then all those sages surrounded the bull among men and sat down, honouring him, like the seven sages the pole star.
And they asked the unconquered king the purpose of his entering the hermitage.
[The king said:] "I am a king named Viradyumna, known in all quarters; I have come to the forest to seek my lost son Bhuridyumna.
He was an only son, best of Brahmanas, a child, sinless ones; he is not seen in this forest, and I range seeking him."
[Rishabha said:] When the king had said this, the sage bowed his head and was silent there, and did not answer the king.
For the Brahmana had once been not much honoured by that king, and, wasted by hope, king of kings, had undertaken long austerity.
I will never accept gifts from kings, nor from other classes, so he had resolved then in mind.
Hope makes a man, a child, babble, standing by; I shall remove it, so he had resolved.
[The king said:] "What is the thinness of hope, and what here on earth is hard to obtain? Let the blessed one say this, for you see dharma and wealth."
[Rishabha said:] Then the blessed Brahmana, thin of body, thin, as if remembering all that, said to the king:

There is nothing, king, equal to hope in thinness; because of its hard attainment, I sought kings.
mahabharata:12:126.36	[The king said:] 'Thin and not thin I have understood from your words, Brahmana; and its hardness of attainment, like the word of the Veda, twice-born.
mahabharata:12:126.37	But a doubt has arisen in my heart, greatly wise one; it is for you, best of men, to answer me truly as I ask.
mahabharata:12:126.38	What is thinner than you? Let the blessed one say this; if it is no secret, Brahmana, what in this world is hard to obtain?'
mahabharata:12:126.39	[Krishatanu said:] 'Nothing is hard to obtain, or if so, one who seeks would gain steadiness; harder to find, dear one, is he who does not slight a seeker.
mahabharata:12:126.40	Not helping another as one is able, as is fitting, after promising—the hope attached to all beings is thinner than I.
mahabharata:12:126.41	A father with one son, when the son is lost or gone abroad, who does not know his state—that hope is thinner than I.
mahabharata:12:126.42	In the childbearing of women, in the sons of the aged, and, lord of men, the hope of the wealthy—that is thinner than I.'
mahabharata:12:126.43	[Rishabha said:] Hearing this, king, the king with his household, touching his feet with his head, fell before the best of the twice-born.
mahabharata:12:126.44	[The king said:] 'I propitiate you, blessed one; I wish for a reunion with my son. Choose a boon, Brahmana, whichever you wish, as is fitting.'
mahabharata:12:126.45	[Rishabha said:] And the lotus-eyed king said to him: 'This is true, as you have said, Brahmana; there is no falsehood in it.'
mahabharata:12:126.46	Then, laughing, the blessed Tanu, best of upholders of dharma, quickly brought his son by austerity and learning.
mahabharata:12:126.47	Having brought that son, he then chided the king, and Dharma, best of upholders of dharma, showed himself.
mahabharata:12:126.48	Having shown himself, divine and wonderful to see, free of sin and anger, he went to the forest from near.
mahabharata:12:126.49	This I saw, king, and thereafter heard the words; quickly remove this hope, thinner still.
[Bhishma said:] "Thus addressed there by the great-souled Rishabha, great king, Sumitra then quickly removed that thinner hope.
So you too, son of Kunti, hearing these words of mine, be steady, king, like Himavan, best of mountains.
You are a seer and a hearer in hard matters done for gain here; having heard me, great king, you should not grieve."

Having reached the mountain Pariyatra, there was a great hermitage of Gautama; hear also the time Gautama lived there.
mahabharata:12:127.4	For sixty thousand years that Gautama practised austerity; that sage, steady in fierce austerity, nourished by austerity,
mahabharata:12:127.5	tiger among men, was approached then by Yama, guardian of the world, who saw the sage Gautama of fine austerity.
mahabharata:12:127.6	Recognising Yama who had come in splendour, that Brahmana sage, rich in austerity, approached him, self-controlled, with joined palms.
mahabharata:12:127.7	Seeing him, the king of dharma saluted that bull among men and invited him with dharma, saying, 'What shall be done?'
mahabharata:12:127.8	[Gautama said:] 'By doing what may one be freed from debt to mother and father, and how does a man enjoy the hard-to-reach auspicious worlds?'
mahabharata:12:127.9	[Yama said:] 'Honouring mother and father day by day, directly, should be done by one devoted to austerity and purity, and ever delighting in truth and dharma.'

For one whose helpers are wicked ministers, whose counsel is leaked on all sides, who is falling from his kingdom and sees no other course,
mahabharata:12:128.3	who is invaded by an enemy host, hard to reach, by one stronger, whose realm is unprepared, who disregards place and time,
mahabharata:12:128.4	when conciliation cannot be had, or division by too much oppression, or life for the sake of wealth—what merit would there be there?
[Bhishma said:] "You have asked a secret dharma, bull of the Bharatas, exceedingly so; unasked I would not venture to speak of this dharma, Yudhishthira.
Dharma is subtler than speech and intellect, bull of the Bharatas; having heard and attended it with good conduct, one sometimes becomes good.
By deed with forethought one may or may not become rich; such is this question, and it must be settled by your intellect.
Hear the expedient, full of dharma, for the journey of life, Bharata; I do not wish such a dharma for the sake of dharma; taking from the wealthy here is painful, but afterwards held fit.
Having followed the certainty of all the courses, the more a man constantly studies the scripture, the more he knows, and his knowledge pleases him.
Having reached this expedient dharma practised by people before, there is one dharma for the capable and another in calamities, Bharata.
Dharma is called the first treasury; intellect is weightier than dharma; having obtained dharma, the weak do not find a just livelihood.
Since wealth is not wholly obtainable, therefore even adharma is heard of in calamity as a mark of dharma.
That in which adharma is born—so the wise know; you doubt whether it is next to the kshatriya.
How his dharma may not decline and how he may not fall into the enemy's power—that is what must be done here, they say; one should not let oneself sink.
A sunken self is not for dharma, nor for another, nor for itself; by all means one should lift oneself up—that is the decision.
In that, dear one, the decision of those who know dharma lies in skill in dharma; effort and livelihood in the kshatriya come from the strength of arms, so it is heard.
When livelihood is blocked, whom may a kshatriya not take from, other than ascetics and Brahmanas, Bharata?
As a Brahmana in distress may sacrifice for one not fit to sacrifice and eat food not fit to eat, so this too; there is no doubt.
For one afflicted, what is no door? Or the path of one restrained? When he is afflicted he runs out where there is no door.
By the decay of his treasury and strength, there is the ruin of all the world; begging is not prescribed, nor the livelihood of Vaishya or Shudra.
Livelihood next to one's own dharma, for one who does not live by others', bearing first the primary course, is living by a substitute.
Living unjustly in calamity from the dharmas is seen even among Brahmanas when livelihood has failed.
What doubt can there be in the kshatriya? This is ever settled: he may take from the eminent and should never sink.
They know the kshatriya as the slayer and protector of the subjects; therefore a kshatriya protecting should take.
Apart from violence, king, no one here has a livelihood—not even a lone sage ranging, risen from the forest.
One cannot live the livelihood of Shankha and Likhita, especially, best of the Kurus, wishing to protect the subjects.
Mutual protection by king and realm in calamity should be ever practised here; this is the eternal dharma.
As the king protects the realm in calamities with floods of wealth, so in distress the king should be protected by the realm.
Treasury, army, rod, friends and anything else amassed—the king should make no gap in the realm when it is overrun by hunger.
Seed must be provided with food, so those who know dharma say. On this they tell the teaching of Shambara of great illusion.
Fie on the life of that king in whose realm the lowest man sinks for lack of livelihood, who knows the words of Shibi.
The treasury and strength are the root of the king; the treasury is the root of strength; that is the root of all dharmas, and the subjects are rooted in dharma.
The treasury cannot be had here without oppressing others; how then strength? For that purpose, having oppressed, he is not liable to blame.
Even what should not be done is done for sacrifice in the sacrificial acts; for this reason a king is not liable to blame.
One thing is for the sake of wealth, another contrary, another for the sake of non-wealth; all that is the mark of wealth; thus the wise should see by intellect the decision about the task.
One thing is for the sake of sacrifice, another is not for sacrifice, and another is for the sake of the aim of the sacrifice; all that is a means of sacrifice.
I shall give an illustration here that shows the truth of dharma: those who obstruct cut the sacrificial post for the sacrifice,
and certain neighbouring trees they surely cut too; and they, falling, strike other trees.
So those men who obstruct a great treasury—without slaying them I see no success here, scorcher of foes.
By wealth both this world and the next are conquered; truth and the word of dharma are not so for the poor.
By all means one should take wealth for the purpose of sacrifice; the fault is not equal in what is to be done and not done, Bharata.
These two do not arise, king, in any way, Bharata; I see no one anywhere in the forests grown rich.
Whatever wealth is seen here on earth, this man desires, 'May this be mine, may this be mine.'
There is no dharma equal to kingship, scourge of foes; they declare the dharma of kings for calamity otherwise than this.
Some gather hoards of wealth by gifts and deeds, others by austerity as ascetics, and others by intellect and skill.

They call the wealthless weak; by wealth one becomes strong; all is attainable by the wealthy; the possessor of a treasury crosses all; from the treasury come dharma and desire, and this world and the next."

Of one whose chiefs are suspected, whose counsel is leaked, Bharata, whose friends are not to be reckoned on, whose ministers are everywhere divided,
mahabharata:12:129.3	who is invaded by an enemy host, weak against the strong, of distressed mind—tell me what remains to be done.
[Bhishma said:] "If he is an outsider seeking conquest, skilled in dharma and wealth, pure, he should make peace quickly, releasing the earlier ones first."
And I did that deed by which this son of mine died; let Time and Death go; release the serpent, Arjunaka.
All kings then came under his sway, for he became their emperor by his conduct and strength.
Good luck to you, Yadavi mother, hear this word of mine: I have lived happily, son, well cared for by you.
By the sinner Kritavarman, with the help of Drona's son, his life is ended today, and his fame too, fair-waisted one.

[Indra said:] "In the world of heaven there is no place for those with dogs; the wrathful spirits take away offerings and gifts; therefore consider and act, king of dharma; abandon the dog; there is no cruelty in this."
And the king, son of Dharma, took up fierce anger, and Yudhishthira reproached the gods and Dharma too.
